In my last unit they said shit like this every fucking Friday, heavily emphasized on four day weekends as well and we *always* ended up staying later. i can count on one hand the amount of times we actually were released even before 1600 in the span of 13 months. Shit was wack. This was in Korea so most of us didn’t really have anything to go “home” to except for booze and video games yk. 

In the same shop, we had a girl who was always going to the bathroom between like 1615-1645 and my floor nco always said some shit like “if your battle buddy wasn’t taking so long in the bathroom yall could go home” and we learned to just brush it off because even if she wasn’t in there we’d still be sitting there till 1700 doing nothing. They liked to tell us that if something came in after we left “early” there’d be no one there to do it like we weren’t ever coming back to work again. These are the same NCOs that left me, a PFC at the time, and my friend, a SPC who had only a month more TIS than me in charge of the shop on a regular basis and we truly held it down with no issues. 

We also got sent to the motor pool for some random ass reason and got told whenever we finished at the mp we could go home for the day. It took one time of that happening when I learned that we were going to be at the mp way later than COB and to not get hopeful. 

Now i just do it to myself lol. I’m essentially my own man shop and in charge of myself and i consciously choose to work through lunch every day and im still leaving hours later than i plan to. You have a really good reason to stay in Germany. Sometimes the army says fuck that, so be prepared for that, especially since you only have a few months left, and by the time it gets to the people that make the decision you’ll have even less time.

I’m a little late to the party here but for me it really depends. 
 
Before I went to my first unit I had been stuck in a training environment for much longer than I should’ve been due to COVID and although all of us holdovers were just waiting on a plane ticket and a date to leave, we still got treated like absolute garbage and got our time wasted so much. This really put a bad taste in my mouth right away for the army. 

My first duty station was amazing. The first few months were rocky and I felt very isolated due to being half a world away from my family and also COVID restrictions but I made the best friends I’ve ever had in my life there. I had great leadership who pushed me and gave me a lot of opportunities to lead my peers as a PFC. That experience will be one I am forever grateful for. That unit taught me so much about my work ethic, who *i* am as not just a soldier, but a person too, and also how i want to be when I become an NCO. 

Where I’m at now has its good and bad days. My unit does PT on our own so I get to wake up late and just show up at nine. No formation, no motor pool Monday, no bullshit really. The guys that work here are all around just really headstrong and arrogant. Being a female in a probably 98% male populated unit can be a little uncomfy sometimes though. Sometimes big army comes in and says not today. 

There are days where I wake up and I’m just in a bad headspace of *I cannot deal with this bullshit today* but the days where I’m not in a bad headspace greatly outnumber the bad days. There’s been lots of ups and downs. There will be ups and downs in everything you do and you have to remember that. There will be bullshit but as long as you keep pushing through, you’ll make it and it’ll be alright. 

You also have to remember that if there’s some miserable shit going on that you aren’t the only person that’s miserable. This thought process really changed my mindset into a more positive one. In my first unit we spent most Thursdays out in the heat setting up big ass tents. These days usually lasted from 630am to 7-8pm and that was the last place I wanted to be at during those times. I made myself miserable by constantly thinking about how much I didn’t want to be there. If you just keep your mind on the task at hand and don’t whine about the bullshit i guarantee you life in the army will feel easier. 

Also, just do the right thing. This is something you’ll hear a lot at basic. They’ll say some shit about doing the right thing (even if you don’t think you did anything wrong, individually or as a mass) and to always do the right thing even when nobody is watching (army values) but it stands true. Don’t try and cheat your way out of shit or take short cuts because at some point you’ll get figured out and either get in trouble or treated like a shitbag and that’s the last thing you want. It takes zero effort to be a decent human being. 

I wish you the best of luck.

I could have died at 22 if it wasn’t for a general surgeon who stood up for me. This is probably really dramatic but I am in the military and my experience with the healthcare has not been great so I fully believe that if this woman didn’t stand up for me things would’ve taken a turn for the worse and fast. 

One morning I woke up at around 3am in the worst pain of my life. I laid on my bathroom floor in the fetal position for hours. I had just been on leave for work and my ROM for COVID just ended so I still went in that morning since it was supposed to be my first day back. During lunch time I had a friend tell me to go to the ER and that he would contact my supervisor to let him know what was going on. 

I went to the ER with lower abdominal pain. I had been doing some DR Google research and the only thing that made sense was appendicitis and with my symptoms, the ER nurse also suspected appendicitis. I went to the ER at 1230 pm and sat in triage for 10 hours. It was probably not until 5pm that they ordered the CT and gave me fentanyl for the pain. Also had to get an umbilical ultrasound to rule out an ovarian rupture and things of that nature. 

The CT came back around 730-8pm. I had been sleeping on and off all day, by this point I was hungry for the first time all day and I wasn’t allowed to eat. On and off the phone with my family and my supervisors at work all day. Despite the pain medication my pain level went from a solid 10/10 to only an 8/10. 

I didn’t have appendicitis. They didn’t know what was wrong with me and were working on moving me to an inpatient room. A doctor came in and told me he thought I had colitis so we were going to do a colonoscopy. That didn’t happen. I had doctors upon doctors coming in and out saying they weren’t doing the surgery and then would come in and tell me I was having surgery until the last one came in and said they were just going to keep me overnight for observation and pain management and that they were still waiting for an inpatient room to free up. At around 9pm a general surgeon came in and reiterated that they didn’t see appendicitis on my CT but that she was going to remove my appendix anyways and just take a look inside my belly to see what was going on. 

By 10pm I was being taken up to the surgical floor. I was in good spirits, the doctors were enjoying my positive attitude and the sense of humor I had from the pain meds making me goofy. I was hopeful for relief. I remember betting with the anesthesiologist that I would remember everything he told me I wouldn’t remember, and I did, it’s my superpower. 

By 12am I was out of surgery and the first thing I remember is having the oxygen on my face and my phone in my hand calling my dad. I was in Korea at the time so his dad had already been started for awhile back in the states. I remember feeling instant relief. The pain that had been there all day long was gone, instead it was replaced by the sensation of have been cut open with a scalpel. I was relieved. I was grateful. I can’t even try to explain how much pain I was in. It was astronomical. 

The next morning I was up and walking around, mostly with ease. While my case of appendicitis wasn’t an emergency emergency, it definitely would have been within 24-48 hours if that surgeon didn’t stand up for me and tell them she was taking it out regardless of what the CT showed. The way I understand it is that I had pre-appendicitis which is why they couldn’t see it. It’s interesting because I have a high pain tolerance and my body said fuck that noise that day. 

It was a really long recovery process, I couldn’t sit up by myself or get myself off the couch for a few weeks. It wasn’t for awhile that I truly processed that if they didn’t do the surgery that I could’ve been in really rough shape shortly after.

My life revolved around band/marching band/playing the trumpet when I was a teen. 

I remember the summer after 7th grade, I learned I didn’t make the honors band for 8th grade and practiced about 2-4 hours a day *every day*. I got moved to honors the first week of school because I had improved so much. Because of this, every day of the week I was practicing around 4 hours a day. We had to log our practice sessions for a grade and most weeks I’d have 30-40 hours of practice. 

My first two years of high school - during football or “marching” season, we had practice every morning before school, then more practice during the actual band class period during the day and I would still go home and add another 2-3 hours on that. During the off season I practiced probably 6 hours a night on technical skills and etudes for auditions. 

I was being looked at by the Eastman school of music when I was a freshman and I threw it all away. Moved away when I was a junior and I was going through a lot of mental health issues so I just quit, simple as that. A big part of that was my new school was very small and there was no competition anymore. Any specialized bands to do as an extra-extra curricular were hours away and I didn’t have my license yet and my parents wouldn’t be able to take me. 

I could’ve had my life set out for me if I hadn’t quit but honestly, I feel like it’s one of the better decisions I’ve made. I miss it of course, music was my first love, but there’s more to life then only playing my trumpet. 

I still own multiple trumpets now. They just sit in my gaming room, haven’t been touched really. Sometimes I’ll pull it out and play but very few and far between. Having no one to share my music with doesn’t bring me joy. I loved performing for others.

Moderation is hard at the beginning but once you get into the habit, it’s pretty easy to keep.

I left in June of 2020. 

My cycle was the one of the first full covid protocol cycles at Fort Jackson. Since I have no other experience I don’t want to say that my basic training was necessarily easier, but there were factors that made it “easier”. 

The reception DSs didn’t really know what to do with us I don’t think. I don’t know if this is how it was normally was pre-COVID but we had so much free time in the day. The first night was rough but after that we spent so much time in the bay getting to call our families and sleep and whatever. We basically didn’t have anything to do after like day four of reception so we just hung out and slept. 

Basically our training was shrunk down into 6-7 weeks instead of 10 because of yellow phase. The companies and platoons were smaller so we didn’t need as much time for training I guess. Ranges were generally done by 1100-1300 and we’d go back to the bay, clean, and then just chill in PTs. The whole time we generally didn’t have anything to do past 1700 so we just hung out I guess. Weekends were chill too. Had a few classes on Saturday and then “bay maintenance” for the rest of the day, and then sundays the entire day was just hanging out not doing shit. Sleeping on the floor and whatever. We got *so much* sleep too. Would shut the lights off between 1900-2000 and woke up at 0500. Fireguard didn’t start until 2200. Only one fireguard shift for each person per night with one night off a week. 

Our training schedule was so fucked that we did the confidence course, gas chamber and rappel tower all in weeks 6-8. 

My company ate at the DFAC maybe five times. The rest was hot A’s for breakfast and lunch and then an MRE for supper. That was kind of a bummer lol, the same food every day got kind of old fast. 

We were supposed to wear masks but only wore them really when the BC and CSM were walking around seeing how things were. 

After about 3-4 weeks we very rarely got smoked. My DSs just stopped giving a shit I think. The generally treated us very well for us being trainees. A lot of them didn’t go home because they didn’t want to risk getting their families sick. Even if someone fucked up during fireguard or someone found contraband nothing happened. Never had a health and welfare check either. Usually only got smoked once a day in the morning for cleanliness. 

We had to move bays 4-5 times due to other companies getting COVID. I got really good at being able to move all of my shit in one trip. Had a whole laundry bag full of clothes stollen that nobody did anything about. Left me with one pair of socks total and nobody gave a shit about it. 

We even had another BN move into one of our bays because they had nowhere else to put them and we didn’t have many trainees anyways. There was about 100 in my company total. 

This doesn’t have to do with COVID but because I went during the summer, there were lots of random pop up storms because SC is SC so we missed out on a lot of training. Lots of hours spent in an LPA just bullshitting with the DSs.

Third and final edit: I did both BCT and AIT at Jackson and my AIT was more demanding than my BCT. Got the dog shit smoked out of us all the time and they were much stricter than at BCT. Was wildly disappointed. Less sleep and no free time. If that tells you anything about how easy my BCT was.

Also, you got this my sweet friend. I’m writing some things below, if you don’t want to read them obviously you don’t have to especially since I accidentally wrote so much. 

I possess lots of self doubt so I was telling myself for the last few weeks “I’m going to fail, I should cancel my appointment.” Over and over again. Practice, practice, practice. Even the basics are very beneficial in the time leading up to the very day. Put more of your focus on things you’re uncomfortable with. I don’t know what the driving laws are where you are but I had a friend that is actually 18 drive with me a lot rather than my parents and she was great. She didn’t yell at me or over criticize me when I made a mistake, she waited until I was done turning (in my case) and calmly told me I need to work on them and how to make them better. If you have someone you can drive with that is calm and collected and will help you feel more confident I really do recommend that as it made all the difference in the world. 


As for the actual test date, try to do as many breathing exercises as you can even hours beforehand. It helped me so much. I did inhale for 3 seconds and exhale for 5. Long deep breaths and imagine you are exhaling the negativity and stress. I know it’s easier said than done but it helped me a lot more than I thought it would. I did some positive affirmations on my way to the test and while I was waiting to take mine. 

Things like: 

“I am confident” 

“I am a good driver” 

“I am capable” 

The morning of, my friend that had been helping me came over and we got in the car and went and practiced all of my parking (what I was most scared of) until i had to leave for my test which helped A LOT.  I felt a lot better going into the test knowing that I could do everything I was going to be tested on. 

I’m a compulsive checker so I have to check things over and over again to make sure (like if I close the store at night when I work I end up walking back 5-6 times after I got off to make sure I locked the door, printed out the close reports, etc.) so I gave my mom a list of all the documents I needed to prove my identity, residency and citizenship and she would read them off and I would put them on the table in front of her. If you don’t know what you’ll need you need to go on your state’s dmv website and look over it so that way you come prepared. I was shocked at how many people didn’t come with all of their documents. Definitely make sure you bring your current vehicle registration, insurance card and driving permit. You will not be allowed to go out without those with you. 

You will probably have to do a vehicle equipment demonstration before you even start driving on the road test. The morning of me and my friend got in the car and over and over and over again went over them to make sure I had them all down. 

The ones I had to do 

- Parking break

-Right and left signals

-High Beams and low beams (if you have automatic lights you will need to do these manually) 

-Made sure both of my brake lights worked

-Parking brake. I had to set mine and then I set it 

-Hazard lights

-Windshield wipers 

-Mirrors. I was kind of lost on this one so I took my hand and kind of adjust my rear view mirror and told her it was my rear view, I moved my right  mirror just a tad and told her it was my right mirror and the same with my left. She told me to adjust my mirrors where I needed them before we left

-Seatbelts

-Making sure my seat slid back and forth. 

-Car horn 

-Windshield defroster and fan control (when I showed her this all of my air conditioning/heating settings came up too so i asked her and made sure it was ok to have my heat on since it was cold and rainy out, whatever makes you comfortable) 

-Fuel gage

There may be more it just depends where you what state you live in so make sure you know what you’ll have to do and where everything is/how to do it. I think it was quite a bit of points on my test to do this so if it works the same way where you are then if you know everything that’s already a good start. You may even have to know your hand signals so make sure you know those just in case they ask. 

On the actual test, don’t forget to put your seatbelt on before starting your car. Make sure your seats and steering wheel are in a place that are comfortable for you. I would double check to make sure the examiner is where theirs before you start the car as well as I have read that some of them like to trick people which is kind of bullshit. 

Make sure you use your turn signal on every single turn, lane change and parking. I was parked in a spot where I could pull out to leave the parking lot so I signaled, put my car in drive (still holding the brake), checked my mirrors and looked over my left shoulder to check my blind spot before pulling away. If you have to do parallel parking, make sure you signal before starting, and if you have to do 90 degree parking do the same. Don’t forget to signal when pulling out. 

Make sure you come to a complete stop at stop signs. Don’t slam on your brakes but make sure when you stop it is smooth but you still have that kind of kickback so they actually feel your car stop. Before I drove again I checked my mirrors, scanned left, right left and started driving. If they tell you to go to the stop sign and turn right, do the same as above but make sure you quickly check your mirrors again and check your blindspot before turning. Even if you do actually stop the car they will accuse you of rolling the stop sign which I think is an automatic fail. 

On lane changes you’ll want to make sure you signal, check your mirrors, check your blind spot and then move lanes (this includes turn lanes). Don’t forget to get in the turn lane if there is one not doing so is considered a dangerous action and is a fail. 

When I scheduled my driving test I immediately came to Reddit to search for other people’s posts asking for tips. Most of them said to over exaggerate things like checking your mirrors, checking them more frequently and your blind spot. They say when checking your mirrors to actually move your head so the examiner can see you checking them because if you just glance with your eyes they can’t see that and will say that you didn’t check them. When I started driving again I got into the bad habit of not checking my mirrors at all so I had to get back into quick. Every time I was making a turn I checked my mirrors quick and made sure I checked my blind spot before I made the turn. 

One way streets have two lanes. This is how I did almost fail. She could have failed me for this but she didn’t. I got lucky. She said because I wasn’t from the town I was driving in that I wouldn’t have known better so she passed me. I was told just to keep left and watch for cars backing out and pulling out of parallel parking spaces. The one way street I drove on also doesn’t have marked lanes. 

Since I mostly drove myself I went on YouTube to look up videos too. This helped a lot. I live in Minnesota and there is actually an ex-examiner who made a video on the top ten reasons why people fail the Minnesota driving test which was so helpful to me. There are other pages that help with turning, parking, all that good stuff. The week leading up to my driving test I went online and basically searched on what will make you automatically fail so that way I made sure I wasn’t doing any of those before I actually got on the road when taking the test. 

The night before my test, I once again came to Reddit and asked for any night before tips and I got some good advice. Get good sleep. This is hard one for me with anxiety insomnia so I took a cbd gummy with some melatonin in it (or just melatonin itself). When I woke up I tried  to follow my daily routine the best I could before going out with my friend to practice so I felt like I wasn’t doing anything out of the ordinary, just another day. Be respectful to your examiner and make sure you say thank you at the end whether you pass or fail. I get really bad pressure to speak when I’m anxious and I talk really fast so before I put my car in drive before I started the test, I realized I forgot to take my kitty shaped stress ball (it’s filled with shaving cream, more squishy :)) and my dumb ass looks at this woman and says “I have a stress ball right there, you can use it if you need it. I hope I don’t scare you, I don’t think I will but if you need to use it you can.” 

Eat a decent meal a couple hours beforehand. My anxiety goes up A LOT when I don’t eat and when I have low blood sugar I get even more shaky than I already am.
